Does picking up new languages get easier as you learn more? What language took the most work for you to learn?

Does picking up new languages get easier as you learn more?

Absolutely.

What language took the most work for you to learn?

For the vast majority of people, that will be the first foreign language they learn, for the reason of the previous question. It certainly was true for me : English was the hardest.

The reason is that while you only speak one language, you don't make the difference in your head between semantics and concepts. It means for example, you can't separate the concept of a chair from the word chair. The same goes with whole sentences. Once you know at least one foreign language well enough, you can make that separation and link many different words, syntax and grammar rules directly to the concepts they represent. Add that to the fact that many languages have similar grammar concepts, and once you've learnt how it works once, you only have to apply the difference in its application to fit a new language.

I have a few different questions.

1) How old were you when you started developing the ability to speak each of these languages?

2) Most people claim that it is easier for younger persons to become fluent in a new language. Is this true? If so, what age would be the cut-off in terms of the most significant increase in difficulty?

3) When taking both French and Spanish courses in college, I found it helpful to immerse myself in these new languages by interacting with friends and co-workers who also had the ability to hold basic conversations in these languages. I even started playing French-language versions of MMORPGs, so that I would be forced to put my skills to use every evening. I was the top student in my language courses because of these efforts. So, my question is, what methods did you personally implement that provided assistance in learning new languages?

4) This one is for fun: Why Esperanto? How often do you use this language? Do you think it will make a come-back? Do you hope it will make a come-back? Are there any benefits to knowing how to speak this language? If so, what are they?

1. How old were you...
    • French from birth;
    • English from the fourth grade, so around 9 years old;
    • Spanish in my second year of CÉGEP, so 18;
    • Italian when I met my SO, I was 23;
    • German I don't remember when I actively started, I must have been about 27 or 28;
    • Esperanto, 31;

  2. .... it is easier for younger persons...

    This is a complex question to which a quick answer is both yes and no, as far as I'm aware. It's easier for children to develop near native fluency, meaning one wouldn't know it wasn't their first language, but it will take them way longer to actually master it than an adult would, because an adult will actively study it and develop strategies to get to his/her goal.

    Adults, although they certainly will keep a foreign accent all their lives, are capable of learning a language until they die. And most will quit before because they're heard this myth that they can't learn something new at their age, when in fact, they would have encountered the same difficulties no matter at what age they started, they would simply have persevered had they been younger, it's a self fulfilling prophecy : "I can't do it because I'm old, therefore, I don't put the efforts in, proving my point". But someone can be very well understood even if they have an accent. Adults generally learn way faster, but it's only because they don't learn the same way, they usually learn actively, while children learn passively (by imitation).

    In this perspective, I've recently seen a very interesting TEDx talk about one simple rule to learn any language.

  3. What methods did you...

    I talked to people. I didn't stress vocabulary acquisition (in the sense of drilling vocabulary lists by heart), I made sure I understood the grammar, and especially the pronunciation, then ran with it. You can check the translation of a word in a few seconds in a dictionary, it's not hard. But you can't do that with a grammar concept or the pronunciation of a particular sound that doesn't exist in your native language. It's not that hard to carry around a dictionary while traveling, especially now with smart phones and all. So as soon as I could say a few sentences like "how do we say X in Y language?", I was good to go.

    I didn't do the same things with all my languages though, you can see I learned them at different periods of my life and I gained in wisdom while I grew up. For Spanish, although it wasn't the primary goal, I went for a one month solo trip in Spain while I only had had two classes of Spanish in college. I was bad, but I stuck to it, always preferring Spanish over French or English, that would have been the easy way out, for everything : tourist information, guided tours, speaking with hostel clerks, etc. By halfway through the trip, I was interpreting between English and Spanish for a couple from Australia (my second and third languages) for an hotel reservation over the phone. By the end of the month, someone asked me if Spanish was my native language. I wasn't all that good, but since I had mastered the pronunciation, I just talked faster to hide my grammar mistakes. The thing is, I spoke faster than I could understand, and people, hearing me speak like that, didn't hold back to articulate. It got hard, it got ugly, and boy did I learn!

  4. Why Esperanto?

    Short answer : why not?

    Long answer : because I had learned about it and I found the idea fascinating. Also the fact that it's so easy to learn and scientific studies showed that learning Esperanto as a first foreign language made the next ones easier, even in the same time. They took 2 groups, one learning French for four years, and one learning Esperanto for one year and then French for the remaining three. The group who had learnt Esperanto was better at French despite having studied it one year less.

    I actually barely started to learn it and I'm still concentrating on German, so it may take longer than if I concentrated on it. And accordingly, I don't speak it much as of now.

    I don't think it ever diminished in interest, so I don't know if we can speak of a come-back. I think the idea behind it is interesting (taking the politics out of language), and many people don't realize that, even if it's a made up language, it's not more or less monitored than most natural languages. It's been around long enough that it has acquired a culture, some children being raised in Esperanto, and enough people speaking it to have the language shift like any natural language. Do I hope it gets more attention and becomes more prominent? I think it would be nice, but I'm not holding my breath. If it catches on (more than currently), that's a good thing, but I wouldn't fight for it. For me, at least for now, it's just for fun. But eventually I will try and use it anytime I have the occasion.

Adults, although they certainly will keep a foreign accent all their lives

Really? Even if they work at it consciously? Because it seems to me that accents happen because people are combining their native language and the foreign one.

It's not as easy as that. Of course it can be done, but the amount of effort needed is astronomical, and for what exactly? When you could spend that time learning three other languages?

I've met many people living in a country for 50+ years and still having an accent, even a foreign accent of their native language (e.g. someone from France keeping their France accent after living in French Canada). The accent is not huge, though, just a hint, the way a certain sound is made that even a native would have trouble describing properly what sounds off.

If your original language had all of the sounds of the language you're trying to learn, you can eventually speak without an accent, or very close to it. But many languages simply don't use certain noises, and so get them mixed up or can't hear or say them correctly (think asians with L and R, or Americans with the dozens of additional vowel sounds in swedish).

Where do I start?

Also what do you think of Rosetta Stone?

Thanks for doing this!

First off, I've already given some advise in the first AMA I did in the other subverse, to someone who wanted to learn Japanese. Most of what I said to them can be applied to you as well.

First thing first, you need to pick a language, and try to stick with it until you learn it well. You can base your choice on your interest for the culture of the people who speak it, or your interest in visiting the places where it is spoken. If you have friends or family who speak it, it may be easier to keep you motivated. I don't think choosing a language based on perceived difficulty to learn it is a good idea. What will make you learn it is motivation, no matter how easy or hard it is.

And the first foreign language is always the hardest, so don't despair. It will be hard, it will take lots of time. But it's not a race. Take pauses from learning if you feel overwhelmed, and persevere. At one point, you'll have that click where you'll feel you can make a sentence without looking in a dictionary, and you'll understand a good deal of what people are saying. Passed this point of immense satisfaction, it'll feel like a soft ride (a long one, but without the frustration of the beginning).

I haven't tried Rosetta Stone myself. But what I heard about it is that it's quite expensive for what it is. And most people don't find it that much effective, especially considering the price. If I were you, I'd take that amount of money and find a regular class to attend to. Nothing beats a live teacher, especially in the beginning, and especially for the first foreign language.

But I found that language classes in school, at least up until high school, were next to useless. Teachers usually are not the best, and most students are attending for the sole purpose of getting a good grade, passing the exam, and move on with their lives. The ones who actually want to learn are rare, whereas in a private class, everyone is there because they want to learn, and the real benchmark is your ability to speak, not a grade on a piece of paper.

I'll still repeat the most important points from the advise I gave to the Japanese learning guy/gal :

  • Learn how to pronounce sooner rather than later. This is a primordial skill and it's hard to reverse once you learn a bad habit;
  • Learn grammar. The hard points, for English natives, are usually : genders, cases (for German), verb conjugations, word order, prepositions, agreement.
  • Focus on the two points above, vocabulary will come naturally with practice and while learning the other points, and you'll retain it more easily than if you learned lists by heart.
  • If you do want to learn vocabulary, learn its etymology with it, or at least a mnemonic (some pun or stuff that helps the memory). If you know where a word comes from, it helps a lot in remembering it, and it can help with English spelling as well as a bonus, especially if you opt for French.
